Cup of Wrath
kŭp ŭv rôth
n. phrase (the figure of God's judgment as a cup given to be drunk)
The image is one of the oldest in Scripture: judgment handed to a man in a vessel, so that he must take it into himself. Christ takes the figure up in Gethsemane and asks for it to pass.

Biblical Definition

“For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them” (Psa 75:8). Jerusalem “hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury” (Isa 51:17). Jeremiah is handed it for the nations: “Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations… to drink it” (Jer 25:15). It is poured “without mixture” at the last (Rev 14:10). And in the garden: “O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt” (Mat 26:39).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines cup as a small vessel used to drink out of; and, in Scripture, sufferings and afflictions, or the portion of blessings or of judgment allotted to a person.

expand to see more

CUP, n. A small vessel, used commonly to drink out of.

2. The contents of a cup; the liquor contained in a cup, or which it may contain.

3. In a Scriptural sense, sufferings and afflictions; that which is to be received or endured.

4. Also, blessings and favors.

Key Scripture

Psa 75:8 — "For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them."

Isa 51:17 — "Awake, awake, stand up, O Jerusalem, which hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury; thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling, and wrung them out."

Jer 25:15 — "For thus saith the LORD God of Israel unto me; Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send thee, to drink it."

Rev 14:10 — "The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb:"

Mat 26:39 — "And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt."

Modern Corruption

Gethsemane is read as fear of the nails, and the Old Testament had already defined what a cup in God's hand contains.

expand to see more

The agony in the garden is often explained as a brave man's dread of crucifixion, which raises a difficulty nobody answers: martyrs since have gone to worse deaths singing, and it would be strange for the Lord to face His less well than His servants faced theirs. The figure He used tells what He was looking at. A cup in the hand of the LORD is a fixed image in the prophets and it never means physical pain; it means the undiluted fury of God poured out on the guilty, drunk to the dregs. What made Him sweat as it were great drops of blood was not the Roman procedure but the contents of that cup.

The doctrine of substitution is the whole of the difference between the two readings. If He drank the cup, then the wicked of Psalm 75 who must wring out the dregs are the very people He drank for, and the exchange is total — His people receive instead the cup of blessing which we bless (1Co 10:16), and the same night He handed them one. Two cups sit side by side at the end of that evening: the one He took and the one He gave.

Revelation 14:10 keeps the doctrine from sentimentality by describing what remains for those who do not receive the exchange: wine of the wrath of God, poured out without mixture, undiluted. In this age every judgment is mixed with mercy and men mistake the dilution for the drink. The garden is the measure of what the undiluted cup is, and the measure is a Man on His face in the dirt asking whether there is any other way.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kos (H3563), a cup; chemah (H2534), fury, heat; shemarim (H8105), dregs, lees; Greek poterion (G4221), cup; akratos (G194), unmixed.

expand to see more

Hebrew kos (H3563) — cup; Psalm 75:8, 11:6, 16:5, Isaiah 51:17, 51:22, Jeremiah 25:15.

Hebrew chemah (H2534) — fury, hot displeasure; Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15, Psalm 6:1.

Greek poterion (G4221) — cup; Matthew 26:39, 20:22, John 18:11, 1 Corinthians 10:16, Revelation 14:10.

Usage

"“In the hand of the LORD there is a cup… the dregs thereof” — what the figure always means."

"“Let this cup pass from me” — not the nails, the contents."

"“Poured out without mixture” — what is left for those without the exchange."
